implementation_notes: java.util.stream is the library realization: a stream pipeline is a source, zero or more lazy intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct) and exactly one terminal operation, so stages are lambdas instead of Filter classes and the stream timeline replaces the explicit pipe. BaseStream.parallel() switches the same chain to the common ForkJoinPool, and Collectors materialise the result. Use Flow (or Reactor/RxJava) instead when the stages are asynchronous, run at different rates or must apply backpressure across threads.
code_sketch:
List<Invoice> out = invoices.stream()                 // source
    .filter(inv -> inv.total().signum() > 0)          // stage 1
    .map(this::applyTax)                              // stage 2
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Invoice::date))      // stage 3
    .collect(Collectors.toList());                    // terminal op drives it
pitfalls: A stream can be consumed only once; reusing a closed stream throws IllegalStateException, and intermediate operations never run without a terminal operation.
parallelStream() shares the common ForkJoinPool, so a blocking stage (I/O, locks) starves every other parallel pipeline in the JVM.
Exceptions from a stage surface at the terminal operation with a stack trace that names the lambda, not the failing source record - instrument or unwrap as needed.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent.Flow reactive pipeline
variants.implementation_notes: Flow is the JDK's reactive-streams SPI: a Processor is simultaneously Subscriber and Publisher, so filters form a chain, and demand flows backwards through Subscription.request(n), which is the explicit backpressure the pattern needs when stages run at different rates. JDK-only code requires implementing Publisher/Processor/Subscriber by hand (the request relay is the fiddly part); libraries such as Reactor, RxJava or Akka Streams supply the operator DSL on top of the same contract. Choose it over Stream when the flow is asynchronous, cancellable or bounded by downstream demand.
variants.code_sketch:
SubmissionPublisher<String> pipe = new SubmissionPublisher<>(pool, 256); // capacity = backpressure
pipe.subscribe(new UpperCaseStage());     // Flow.Processor<String,String>
pipe.subscribe(new Sink());               // terminal subscriber requests demand
pipe.submit("record");                    // blocks the producer while the buffer is full
// a stage implements onNext -> transform -> next.onNext and relays request(n)
pitfalls: A subscriber that never calls Subscription.request(n) receives nothing, so the pipeline looks dead even though the publisher is running.
A Processor must forward request(n) downstream and honour cancellation upstream; forgetting the relay either stalls demand or keeps producing after cancel.
Slow subscribers block SubmissionPublisher.submit unless an offer-based overflow policy (drop, latest, buffer) is chosen deliberately.

variants.name: java.nio.channels.Pipe between blocking filter threads
variants.implementation_notes: The classic thread-and-byte-pipe form: java.nio.channels.Pipe yields a one-way channel pair whose sink and source ends are adapted to ordinary streams with Channels.newInputStream/newOutputStream, so each filter runs on its own thread doing blocking I/O and the pipe carries bytes between them. It fits byte-level services with a few long-lived stages where the OS pipe buffer provides the pacing; Stream or Flow fit better for record processing, and a bounded BlockingQueue is a simpler hand-off when both ends live in the same JVM.
pitfalls: A Pipe carries an unframed byte stream, so stage boundaries need their own delimiters or length prefixes.
Only one reader and one writer per pipe are safe; sharing an end across threads needs external synchronisation, and the reader must handle the writer closing mid-stream.
Interrupt state is not propagated by these streams; a filter thread blocked in read() ignores interruption unless the underlying channel is closed explicitly.
